title: Short Stuff: Benin Bronzes
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Benin Bronzes, the art and historical record of the Kingdom of Benin (in present-day Edo State, Nigeria). Covers the kingdom's plaques and bronzes, its contact with Portugal and later European powers as a trading gatekeeper, the 1897 attack on a British trade mission and the punitive expedition that pillaged Benin, the looted objects now held mainly by the British Museum and the Berlin Ethnographic Museum, the repatriation push (including Macron's 2017 report), the planned Edo Museum of West African Art, and the dispute over whether returned works belong to the Oba.
topics: Edo Museum of West African Art

segments.title: Benin Kingdom and early European trade
segments.summary: Josh explains the Benin Bronzes as plaques and artworks made by the Kingdom of Benin to chronicle new obas and queen mothers and major events. Chuck adds that they are also a historical record. The hosts describe Portuguese contact from the fifteenth century, followed by the French, Dutch and English, and how Benin grew powerful as middleman for trade with interior states, including involvement in the slave trade and trade in goods such as ivory and pepper. Britain later sought to cut out Benin as middleman.

segments.title: 1897 attack and British punitive expedition
segments.summary: Chuck describes the January 1897 attack on a British trade mission on the way to Benin City, in which seven British delegates and about 230 African carriers died. Britain launched a retaliatory military expedition that easily overwhelmed Benin. Josh describes the punitive expedition's occupation, the killing of chiefs, the exile of the Oba, and the pillaging of around 10,000 artifacts, including the Benin Bronzes.

segments.title: Looted artifacts and where they are held
segments.summary: The hosts explain the term Benin Bronzes as an umbrella for works in ivory, brass and bronze created from roughly the fifteenth to nineteenth centuries. They discuss the spoils of war, objects distributed to expedition members and sent to the UK, and the largest collections now held by the British Museum and the Ethnographic Museum in Berlin. They cite an estimated value of 130 billion dollars and a 2017 French report commissioned by Macron saying most of Africa's cultural heritage is held outside Africa due to the Scramble for Africa.

segments.title: Repatriation and the Edo Museum
segments.summary: Chuck discusses repatriation efforts, including Macron's pledge to return stolen objects, Germany's involvement, and US institutions such as the Smithsonian and the Met returning looted pieces. Nigeria is set to open the Edo Museum of West African Art, planned for 2025. Josh cites sculptor Hanjazo Gleiley on an artistic awakening in Nigeria from the returns.
topics: Edo Museum of West African Art

segments.title: Ownership dispute over returned bronzes
segments.summary: Chuck names the current Oba, Oba Ewuare II, and notes that in 2023 outgoing Nigerian president Muhammadu Buhari said returned looted items belong to the Oba and his palace. Josh explains Benin's position within Nigeria and the Oba's advisory role. The hosts discuss Western museum discomfort, including comments from museum director Philip Ihenacho, and wonder whether the works will be displayed.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh suggests listeners look up the Benin Bronzes online, and Chuck gives the closing credits.
